North Carolina register of deeds FAQ

Where do I record a deed in North Carolina?

With the register of deeds in the county where the property is located.

Who runs a North Carolina register of deeds office, and what is it for?

Every county's voters pick a register of deeds for a two-year term (NCGS 161-1). Deeds, deeds of trust and the papers that go with them live in that office's public land records. A tax assessor works from a different file, so a change at one counter does not carry to the other.

Besides filing, the register takes two payments: the statewide recording charge, and the deed excise tax that must be paid before a conveyance goes on the record (NCGS 161-10). In an ordinary sale the closing attorney takes the new deed, plus the buyer's loan paperwork, to this counter.

What are the recording fees charged by a register of deeds?

One state statute sets every charge, so the mountains and the coast pay alike. The table lists each charge in the words of NCGS 161-10 prints it.

Statewide charges for common filings
FilingCharge
Deed or other general instrumentPages 1 to 15 together: $26.00. Pages beyond 15: $4.00 each
Deed of trust or mortgagePages 1 to 35 together: $64.00. Pages beyond 35: $4.00 each
Satisfaction or cancellation of a deed of trust or mortgageNo charge
Plat$21.00 a sheet
Certified copyPage one $5.00; each following page $2.00
Document that misses the format rules$25.00 extra
Further instrument inside one document$10.00 each

Payment comes before filing, and the statute treats the list as the whole schedule. Excise tax is a separate bill.

How does the deed excise tax work at the register of deeds counter?

Before the deed is recorded, the seller (the transferor, in the statute's word) pays the tax to the register. NCGS 105-228.30 prices it at one dollar for each $500 of the price or value, rounded up for any fraction.

Land across a county line is handled in the county with the larger share of value. The money divides evenly between county and state, with the state half remitted monthly after refunds and an allowance. Gifts, transfers by will or intestacy and deals where the buyer owes nothing are outside the tax under NCGS 105-228.29.

What should I carry to the register of deeds?

Carry a deed with a completed notary acknowledgment. NCGS 47-14 tells the register not to accept a paper that needs an acknowledgment unless the officer's signature, commission expiration date and any required seal appear on it.

  • The signed instrument with the notary page attached.
  • Letter-size or legal-size paper, with a blank band of three inches across the top of page one.
  • Black print on white stock at 9 points or larger, one side only.
  • The kind of instrument written at the head of the first page.
  • Payment for the recording charge and any excise tax.

Paper that fails these format points is still recorded, with the nonstandard add-on from NCGS 161-14. Where the sole flaw is type smaller than 9 points, a register may waive the add-on if the text is readable.

How fast must the register of deeds record a document?

Papers are registered strictly in arrival order, and each is endorsed with the day and hour it was handed in. The register records on the day of presentation unless a temporary index is running, and permanent indexing must still be done within 30 days (NCGS 161-14).

The stamp carries legal weight. Under NCGS 47-18, a lease running past three years, an option, a right of first refusal or a conveyance is ineffective against lien creditors and purchasers for value until registered, and the order of registration by time sets priority. A buyer therefore wants the deed recorded quickly.

Does a register of deeds accept electronic recording or paper copies of e-documents?

Electronic recording is for approved submitters only. Subsection (a1) of G.S. 47-14 covers e-documents from a federal or state government body and from a trusted submitter, meaning one that signed an electronic recording agreement with that county's register. Ask the office whether your closing attorney is set up.

A paper fallback exists. The register must take a printout of an electronic document if the county has no e-recording, if its system rejects that document type, or if the system is down at the time. A sworn certificate must say the printout is accurate and unchanged. The statute is silent on mailed filings, so telephone before sending anything.

  • Learn which payment forms the office accepts.
  • Put the property address and a return address on a mailed deed.
  • Hold on to the receipt that shows book, page and time.

Can an already recorded paper be recorded again?

Yes, as a rerecording. Mark page one of the earlier instrument, or of a certified copy, in plain view as a rerecording (NCGS 47-14(a)). This helps after a recording mistake has been fixed.

The register can trust the marking and the old recording data without rechecking the acknowledgment or searching for later edits. A corrected deed deserves a lawyer's review before resubmission.

Seals get their own presumption. A record the register accepts is presumed to have borne a clear notary seal image, and the office cannot refuse a record on the ground that the seal misses the notary statute's standard. If a court later finds a seal invalid, anyone who recorded an interest ahead of that finding keeps it.

Which filings count as instruments under the paper-format rules?

The format rules apply to filings that carry a fee under the fee statute. NCGS 161-14(d) names five groups.

  • Instruments in general, which is where a deed falls.
  • Deeds of trust, mortgages, and cancellations of both.
  • Uniform Commercial Code filings.
  • Torrens registrations.
  • Master forms.

Certified copies of court-filed documents and filings that follow the UCC filing-office rules are excused from the paper-size and margin rules.

What if the register of deeds is a party to the document?

A document in which the county's own register is a party can be proved or acknowledged before any magistrate or notary public (NCGS 47-14(e)). Home sales rarely raise this, but it is the one case where the statute names magistrates as acknowledging officers.

What can I do if the register of deeds turns my document away?

A district court judge in the district can order registration. NCGS 47-14(b) gives this route to the person offering an instrument the register declined. The judge must find the signer's execution was proved or acknowledged before an authorized officer and that the officer's signature, commission expiration date and any required seal are present.

The register does not rule on legal sufficiency, so a recorded deed does not prove that it works. Ask an attorney to confirm title before you lean on the record.

More questions about North Carolina Register of Deeds

Which county office takes a deed for my North Carolina house?

The register of deeds where the house stands. For a parcel that crosses a county line, the office in the county with the greater value collects the excise tax and can say how to file.

What does a register of deeds charge for a standard deed?

Up to 15 pages cost $26.00 together, and extra pages are $4.00 each. Excise tax may be due as well, paid at the same counter.

Is there a charge for filing proof that a mortgage was paid?

No. The fee statute lists no charge for a satisfaction or cancellation of a deed of trust or mortgage.

Why would a register of deeds refuse a deed?

Usually because a required acknowledgment does not appear to have been taken before an officer with authority. A district court judge can order registration if the proof or acknowledgment meets the statute.

How soon after I hand in a deed does it appear in the index?

The register is meant to record it the same day. An office using a temporary index must still finish permanent indexing within 30 days after presentation.
